search:followup.overview: A single-term index is a lookup. Real queries are boolean: require all of these, any of these, none of these, or this exact phrase. The phrase query is the one that cannot be answered from term sets alone.
search:followup.task: Extend the document index with boolean and phrase queries, returning sorted document ids for each.
requirements: `QueryIndex` provides `add(doc_id, text)`, `all_of(query)`, `any_of(query)`, `without(query)` and `phrase(query)`, each returning a sorted list of document ids.
Tokens are `text.lower().split()`, with punctuation kept.
`all_of` returns documents containing every token, `any_of` returns documents containing at least one, and `without` returns documents containing none.
`phrase` returns documents containing the tokens consecutively and in that order, including repeated words.
An empty `all_of`, `any_of` or `phrase` returns `[]`. An empty `without` returns every document.
Adding a document that already exists replaces its old content rather than merging into it.

examples.code:
s = QueryIndex()
s.add(2, "a a b")
s.add(1, "a b")
print(s.phrase("a a"))
print(s.without("b"))
examples.explanation: Only document 2 contains the repeated phrase. Both documents contain b, so neither survives exclusion.

search:followup.approach: The boolean queries fall out of set operations on postings lists, and intersecting the smallest list first keeps them cheap. Phrase queries are the real work, because a set intersection cannot see adjacency: a document holding the words `a` then `b` a thousand lines apart is not a match, and an intersection will cheerfully say it is. So you need positions per term, and a phrase is confirmed by walking the positions of the first token and checking that each later token sits at exactly the right offset from it. Starting from the rarest first token is what makes that fast in practice rather than merely correct.
search:followup.note: A phrase match needs consecutive positions, not just the presence of every word. Two tokens appearing far apart in a document are not a phrase, and a plain set intersection will report them as one.

weighted:followup.overview: Single-source shortest path is a standard algorithm. Returning the route rather than the cost, and choosing between equal-cost routes, is what turns this into a problem about tie-breaking.
weighted:followup.task: Find the lowest-cost route to a target from any of several sources, and return the path using a defined tie-break.
requirements: `best_route(graph, sources, target)` returns `(cost, path)`. `graph` maps a string node to a list of `(neighbor, weight)` pairs.
Choose the lowest total cost from any of the sources. `sources` may contain duplicates.
Every weight must be strictly positive, and a `ValueError` is raised if any weight is zero or negative anywhere in the graph, including in components you never traverse.
When several routes share the minimum cost, return the one whose entire node list is lexicographically smallest.
`target` being one of the sources returns `(0, [target])`.
Empty `sources`, or a target that is unreachable, returns `(-1, [])`.

examples.explanation: Both routes cost two; the complete path through a is lexicographically smaller.

weighted:followup.approach: Run Dijkstra once with every source seeded at distance zero, which gives the best cost from any of them. The tie-break is the interesting half, and the tempting approach of comparing whole paths whenever two costs tie does not survive, because a lexicographically smaller prefix can easily lead to a worse complete path. The robust way is to make the comparison part of the state: carry the node sequence in the priority queue key alongside the distance, so the queue always expands the smaller path first, and only settle a node once no later path can be both equal in cost and smaller. That argument needs strictly positive weights, which is why this contract rejects nonpositive ones rather than leaving you to handle zero-cost cycles yourself.
weighted:followup.note: A weight of zero or negative is rejected anywhere in the graph, not only on the route you happen to take. Zero-weight edges are exactly what would make the lexicographic tie-break ambiguous, since a longer path could then tie a shorter one.

rle:followup.overview: A compressed iterator only saves memory if it never expands what it is hiding. This stage keeps that property while adding filtering and a position you can return to, and that position has to mean the same thing whether or not a filter is active.
rle:followup.task: Build a run-length iterator that can filter values, report its position, and be restored to it, all without expanding the runs.
requirements: `ResumableRLE(runs, allowed=None)` iterates `(count, value)` runs of nonnegative count and value. `allowed` is `None`, meaning every value is permitted, or a collection of permitted values.
`next(n)` consumes the next `n` permitted values and returns the last of them, or `-1` once the rest of the stream is exhausted. `n` is at least 1.
Individual values are never expanded and no loop runs per value. Work is proportional to the runs crossed.
`snapshot()` returns `(run_index, offset)`, a position in the original run list rather than in the emitted stream.
`restore(snapshot)` returns to that position, for the same runs and the same filter. Snapshots are opaque to callers.
A run whose value is filtered out is skipped lazily, and skipping it must not change what a position means.

examples.code:
s = ResumableRLE([(3, 2), (4, 9)], allowed={2})
print(s.next(2))
checkpoint = s.snapshot()
print(s.next(1))
s.restore(checkpoint)
print(s.next(1))
examples.explanation: Restoring the snapshot repeats consumption from the same position. The run of 9s is excluded by the filter.

rle:followup.approach: A run is either wholly permitted or wholly filtered, so filtering never splits one, and that is what lets you stay proportional to runs instead of values. Keep an index into the run list plus an offset into the current run, and skip forward over filtered runs without materialising anything. The subtlety is what a position means. A snapshot has to point into the original runs, because the caller has no idea which runs were filtered out and could not reconstruct the position otherwise; a position in the emitted stream would be useless the moment a filter is in play. Copying the runs on construction matters for the same reason, so that restoring a snapshot still means the same thing after the caller has gone and mutated the list.
rle:followup.note: A snapshot is a position in the original run list, not in the stream you have emitted. With a filter in play those are different things, and only the first one can be restored.

nodes.overview: A cluster of nodes learns its own size by exchanging messages over a link that reorders nothing and guarantees nothing: it may duplicate a message, lose it, or deliver it long after it was sent. The interesting part is the harness, because an asynchronous protocol is only testable when something owns the message order, the loss, and the definition of done.
nodes.task: Implement the `Node` and `Channel` classes, `component_sizes`, and `run(net, node_ids, adjacency, rounds)`.
requirements: `Node.known` maps a node id to the set of ids that node has advertised, and starts as `{self: {self}}`. A node learns nothing except by merging a payload.
`Node.merge(payload)` unions the payload in per key and returns the number of ids that were genuinely new. An id advertised by two neighbours is still one node.
`Node.count()` is O(1), because the union of `known` is maintained by `merge` rather than recomputed on demand.
`Node.converged(truth)` reports whether `count()` equals `truth[node_id]`. Convergence is measured against ground truth, never assumed from the loop stopping.
`Channel.send(sender, recipient, payload)` queues a snapshot of an arbitrary payload, and `deliver_all()` delivers everything queued in send order and returns how many messages it delivered.
`Channel.duplicate_every(k)` queues every k-th send twice and `Channel.drop_every(k)` discards every k-th send; `0` disables each. The channel never invents or reorders a message.
`component_sizes(node_ids, adjacency)` returns the true size of the component each node belongs to.

In each round every node sends its **full** known vector to each neighbour, and `deliver_all()` runs before the next round begins. The protocol is the only thing that drives the rounds; nothing else advances `now` or resets the channel.
`run` returns `{"counts", "converged", "rounds"}`, where `rounds` is the number of rounds actually executed. It stops early when a round teaches no node anything new.
`adjacency` is undirected, so an entry in either direction creates the link, and an id in `adjacency` that is not in `node_ids` is ignored.
The rounds argument is a ceiling, not a promise: a well-connected graph converges long before it, and `rounds` in the result is what was actually used.

examples.code:
net = Channel()
out = run(net, ["a", "b"], {"a": ["b"]}, 5)
print(out["counts"], out["rounds"])
examples.explanation: One hop needs one round to carry the claim and a second to show that nothing else arrived.

examples.code:
ids = ["s", "a", "b", "c", "t"]
adj = {"s": ["a", "b"], "a": ["c"], "b": ["c"], "c": ["t"]}
out = run(Channel(), ids, adj, 4)
print(out["converged"], out["rounds"])
examples.explanation: The branch is three hops from s to t, so three rounds carry the news and the fourth only confirms the cluster has stopped changing.

examples.code:
out = run(Channel(), ["a", "b", "x", "y"], {"a": ["b"], "x": ["y"]}, 6)
print(sorted(out["counts"].values()), out["converged"])
examples.explanation: Two components of two nodes each settle on two. Every node is converged and none of them has ever heard of the other component.

nodes.approach: Start with the rule that makes or breaks the problem: a node's answer is a count of the ids in the union it holds, and never the size of the cluster it was told about. Merge is a union per key, so a duplicated message costs nothing and arrival order does not matter. Then decide what `count()` reads. Walking `known` on every call is O(V) per call and O(V^2) per round across the cluster for no information, because merge already knows exactly how many ids arrived; keep the union as its own set, add only the ids that were not already there, and `count()` becomes a set length. The next decision is when to stop. Comparing the total ids learned before and after a round is enough, because a node only ever grows, and it avoids diffing every vector. Be clear that stopping early and being right are different facts, which is why `converged` is computed from `component_sizes` instead of inferred from the loop exiting. On the channel, queue a snapshot rather than the sender's live sets, or a claim can mutate after it was sent and the link delivers something no node said.
nodes.note: The classic wrong answer is a node that falls back to the number of ids in the cluster, or asks around until somebody gives it a number. In a partitioned cluster that turns a correct 2 into a 4. A node may only ever report what it can derive from its own union, which is why the ground truth lives in `component_sizes` and not inside the protocol.

nodes:followup.overview: Full-set gossip gets the right answer and pays for it on every single round: every message carries the whole membership vector, so a settled id is re-sent forever. This stage keeps the same round count and sends only what moved.
requirements: Every node stamps each id with the phase it first heard of it, phase 0 for its own id.
In phase k, a node sends the ids stamped with phase k-1 to each neighbour and nothing else. An id a node already holds is never re-sent in a later phase.
An id that arrives twice keeps the first stamp it was given, which is what keeps the delta a node emits later correct.
`adjacency` is undirected, and an id outside `node_ids` is ignored.
The result is `{"counts", "converged", "sent"}`, where `sent` is the total number of ids transmitted across links.
`converged` compares every count with that node's true component size, so a partition makes the run report non-convergence rather than a wrong number.
`phases` of 0 sends nothing and leaves every node knowing only itself.

examples.explanation: The path is three hops long, so three phases carry the far ends' ids all the way across and every node agrees on four.
Two phases is one hop short of the ends, so the middle agrees and the ends report what they have actually heard.

examples.code: print(gossip(["solo"], {}, 3))
examples.explanation: A node with no links transmits nothing and is trivially correct.

nodes:followup.approach: Give every id a stamp: the phase in which this node first heard of it. That single decision answers both questions the protocol asks. What to send is everything stamped with the previous phase, which is why the stamp has to be taken from the state at the start of the phase rather than read while delivering: an id learned during phase k must not be forwarded in phase k or the delta grows with the cluster instead of shrinking. The stamp also decides when an id stops travelling: once it is older than k-1 it is never sent again, so a node's traffic is bounded by the ids it genuinely did not hold before. Take the first stamp you ever saw for an id and never overwrite it, otherwise a re-advertised id looks freshly learned and is transmitted forever. Cut the delta before you send rather than after, and count the ids you hand to a link, not the messages, because that is the quantity the byte argument is about.
nodes:followup.note: Keep the first stamp. Rewriting it on redelivery looks harmless and turns the delta into the full vector again, because an id re-advertised every phase is stamped with every phase.

resumable.overview: A stream you cannot rewind is a stream you cannot retry. Build a cursor over any source that can say where it is and be put back there, without ever holding the stream in memory, and then compose cursors so a derived stream still means the same thing as the one underneath it.
resumable.task: Implement `Resumable`, three combinators over it, and a JSON object source that survives chunk boundaries.
requirements: `Resumable(source)` wraps a zero-argument callable returning a fresh iterator, or a container that can be iterated more than once. A bare one-shot generator cannot be a source, because there is no way back to its start.
`next(n)` with `n >= 1` pulls exactly `n` items and returns the last, or `-1` if fewer than `n` remain, having consumed the remainder.
The source is never materialised. Constructing the iterator produces nothing, and a `next` call pulls nothing beyond the items it returns.
`snapshot()` is an `int`: how many items have been taken from the source. `restore(pos)` runs the source again and discards items until `pos` items have been taken.
Restoring a position past the end is not an error: the stream is left exhausted and `next` answers `-1` from then on. It costs time proportional to the position, and no buffering.

`chain(a, b)`, `filtered(pred, source)` and `taken(n, source)` each return a new `Resumable` over the underlying source. A derived stream snapshots the position its source does, and restoring it replays the source and re-applies the predicate.
The position counts source items taken, not items handed out, so a filtered stream advances past the items it rejects and its snapshot stays comparable with its source's.
`taken(n, source)` stops after exactly `n` pulls, so its position never runs ahead of `n` and it does not reach for one more item to discover the stream has ended.

`JsonObjects(chunks)` is a re-iterable source of the JSON objects in a `str` or `bytes` stream. Objects straddle chunk boundaries, and braces, backslashes and escaped quotes inside strings are data rather than structure.

examples.code:
r = Resumable(range(1, 6))
print(r.next(2))
position = r.snapshot()
print(r.next(2))
r.restore(position)
print(r.next(2))
print(r.next(1))
print(r.next(1))
examples.explanation: The snapshot counts source items taken, so it is 2 after the first call. Restoring it makes the stream replay 3 and 4 rather than continue from 5, and only the sixth call runs out and returns -1.

examples.code:
made = [0]
def source():
    for i in range(100):
        made[0] += 1
        yield i

r = Resumable(source)
print(made[0])
print(r.next(1))
print(made[0])
examples.explanation: Wrapping the generator produces nothing at all, and one call to next pulls one item. A solution that listed the source up front would print 100 here.

examples.code:
text = '{"a": 1, "t": "x}y"} {"b": {"c": [1, 2]}}'
chunks = [text[i:i + 3] for i in range(0, len(text), 3)]
print(list(JsonObjects(chunks)))
stream = Resumable(JsonObjects(chunks))
print(stream.next(1))
examples.explanation: Three-character chunks split the first object in the middle of its string, where a brace sits. Tracking string and escape state separately from brace depth keeps it together.

resumable.approach: Decide what a position is before writing anything else, because everything else follows from it. A position counts items taken from the source, not items handed out, and that is the only choice that survives composition: with a filter in play the two differ, and a caller cannot reconstruct an emitted-stream position without knowing which items were rejected. Because the position is a count, restore does not need the old output, only the source, so it re-runs the source and throws the first pos items away. That is why the source cannot be a one-shot generator: a generator cannot be rewound, so the only options are to buffer everything it produced, which is the memory you were avoiding, or to require a factory that can run again. Give each combinator a source and rebuild the whole pipeline on restore, so the predicate is replayed rather than skipped, and so `filtered` never has to know how many items its own caller already saw. For the JSON source, keep a buffer, a scan position, a brace depth and two flags for string and escape state, all persisting across chunks; carry the scan position rather than rescanning, and trim the buffer when depth returns to zero so it stays proportional to the object being read.
resumable.note: A position counts source items taken, not items emitted. A filtered stream pulls and rejects items and still advances, so after emitting 2 from range(1, 11) its snapshot is 2, and after emitting 6 it is 6 rather than 3. Restore re-applies the filter from that same source position, which is why the filter is part of what a position means.

resumable:followup.overview: Replaying a source from the start is correct and expensive. This stage replaces it with a bounded window of the recent tail, and makes the limit part of the contract: a position older than the window cannot be honoured, and saying so is better than silently resuming from the wrong place.
resumable:followup.task: Build a log of items whose recent tail can be replayed in memory, with a position that stops being valid at a known point.
requirements: `ReplayLog(window)` keeps an append-only log of items. Only the last `window` items are held in memory; older ones are dropped but still counted.
`append(item)` records one item. `next(n)` with `n >= 1` consumes `n` items and returns the last, or `-1` once the rest is consumed.
`snapshot()` is an `int` position in the whole log, including items that have been dropped.
`restore(token)` moves the cursor to `token` and raises `ValueError` when the item at that position has already fallen out of the window.
`replay(token)` returns the items from `token` to the end of the log as a list and does not move the cursor. It raises `ValueError` on the same condition as `restore`.
`spilled()` reports how many items have fallen out of memory. A reader that falls more than `window` items behind has lost the head of the log.
`window >= 1`, and the log may be empty, in which case `next` returns `-1` and `replay` returns an empty list.

examples.code:
log = ReplayLog(3)
log.append(1)
print(log.next(1))
log.append(2)
log.append(3)
log.append(4)
position = log.snapshot()
print(log.next(2))
print(log.spilled())
log.restore(position)
print(log.replay(position))
examples.explanation: After four appends only the last three are still held, so one has spilled. The position survives because the item it names is still in memory, and replay reads past it without moving the cursor.
The token pointed at the second item, which the window has now dropped. Raising is the honest answer, since the item is not anywhere to be found.

resumable:followup.approach: Keep two things with different lifetimes: a tail of the last window items, and a total count of everything ever appended. A position is an index into the whole log, and the total is what turns that index into an offset into the tail, so a position stays an integer and never has to carry the item it names. The invariant to write down first is that the cursor may fall at most window behind the tail: inside that band reading and restoring both work, and outside it the item is gone, so restore and replay raise instead of returning something plausible. Refusing loudly matters more here than in the base problem, because a reader that silently jumped to the oldest surviving item would process a gap as if it were data. The window size comes from how long a reader can stall before a checkpoint is worthless, and the signal to revisit it is a restore that raises in production, which means a consumer stalled or the window is too small.
resumable:followup.note: A position is an index into the whole log, not an offset into the window. Once the item at that index falls out of the window there is nothing to resume from, and the honest answer is to raise rather than to resume from the oldest item that happens to still be there.

persist.overview: State that survives a restart is a format before it is a data structure. Define the bytes on disk, make the reader able to read an older version of them, and only then decide how the log that holds them behaves when a write is cut off halfway.
persist.task: Implement `RecordCodec` for the format and a `Journal` that replays an append-only log to rebuild the state.
requirements: `RecordCodec.encode(state)` writes a dict of string keys to JSON values as one line prefixed with the schema version, and `decode(text)` reads it back, upgrading an older version on the way.

A missing key and a key holding `None`, `""`, `0` or `False` are different states. All four survive a round trip unchanged, and the encoded text is canonical, so two equal states encode to the same bytes.

`Journal(codec=None)` keeps an append-only log in `self.log`, a list of raw lines. `append(key, value, now)` and `remove(key, now)` each write one line, and `append_raw(text)` writes text exactly as given.

Each entry is a record dict with keys `key`, `value`, `deleted` and `at`. `load(now)` replays the log with the last write for a key winning, a tombstone deleting the key, and anything stamped later than `now` ignored. Stamps are nondecreasing.
A tombstone is a record rather than an absence, which is what lets a delete survive being replayed from an older prefix of the log.
A final line with no terminating newline is a write a crash cut off and is dropped. Any other line that does not decode raises `ValueError`.

`snapshot(now)` returns `{"at": int, "now": int, "data": str}`, the compacted state of the entries visible at `now`. `at` counts the records folded in, and because stamps never decrease those records are a prefix of the log, so that count is a position rather than a guess.
`restore(snapshot, now)` trusts that prefix, replays only the entries after it, and raises `ValueError` when `now` is earlier than `snapshot["now"]`. It does not compact the log.
Every timestamp arrives as an argument. The wall clock is never read, so the same sequence of calls always gives the same result.

examples.code:
c = RecordCodec()
state = {"none": None, "empty": "", "zero": 0, "off": False}
print(c.encode(state))
print(c.decode(c.encode(state)) == state)
print("none" in c.decode(c.encode({"none": None})))
examples.explanation: Keys are sorted so equal states produce identical text. The key holding null is present after the round trip, which is what separates it from a key that was never written.

examples.code:
j = Journal()
j.append("a", 1, now=0)
j.append("a", 2, now=1)
j.remove("a", now=2)
j.append("b", None, now=3)
print(j.load(10))
print(j.load(2))
examples.explanation: At time 10 the tombstone has been applied and the later record is visible, so only b is left. At time 2 the record stamped at 3 has not happened yet, so a was already deleted.

examples.code:
j = Journal()
j.append("a", 1, now=0)
snapshot = j.snapshot(0)
j.append("a", 2, now=1)
print(j.restore(snapshot, 10))
print(j.load(10))
examples.explanation: The snapshot covers the first record and says how many records it folded in. Restoring believes it and replays only what came after, which lands on the same state as a full replay.

persist.approach: Write the encoder and the decoder before the journal, and let the journal write records through the encoder rather than building strings of its own, so there is exactly one place where the format exists. Two decisions drive the rest. First, encode the whole state rather than the interesting keys: dropping falsy values is the tempting optimisation and it destroys the difference between a key that is absent and a key holding null, which no later code can recover. Sorted keys are worth it on their own, because two equal states then encode to identical bytes and a checksum or a diff has something stable to work on. Second, a version in the text turns "the format changed" from a migration weekend into one function per step, and reading a version newer than this code knows is an error rather than a best guess. For the journal, decide the torn-write rule from where the damage can happen: only the last write can be interrupted, so an unterminated final line is dropped and any other bad line is corruption worth refusing. Tombstones are records, not absences, or a delete disappears when the log is replayed from an older prefix. Timestamps come in as arguments throughout, which is what lets a test move time forward by hand and lets a snapshot be replayed at a different time than it was taken.
persist.note: A key holding null and a key that is missing are different states, and so are "", 0 and False. Encode the whole state: anything you leave out is a distinction the format can no longer make. Timestamps are arguments, never a clock, so load(2) and load(10) can differ for the same log.

persist:followup.overview: A newline only tells you a write finished. A checksum tells you the bytes are still the bytes that were written, which moves a different class of damage, corruption in place, from invisible to refused.
persist:followup.task: Frame every record with its own checksum, then make compaction survivable by turning a position into an identity instead of a count of lines.
requirements: `RecordCodec` is unchanged. A log written by either version still reads, and the checksum is computed over the payload `encode` produces.
Each log line is 8 hex digits of crc32 of the payload, a space, the payload, and a newline. `self.log` is the list of raw lines, and `frame(record)` returns that line for one record.
A record is a dict with keys `key`, `value`, `deleted`, `at` and `seq`. The journal assigns `seq`, one per appended record, increasing by one and never reused.
`append(key, value, now)` and `remove(key, now)` write one framed record each. `load(now)` replays with the last write winning and a tombstone deleting the key.

`load(now)` raises `ValueError` when a line does not match its checksum, when a line has no terminating newline, or when a version cannot be read. Unlike the base journal, a torn tail is refused rather than dropped.

`snapshot(now)` returns `{"seq": int, "now": int, "data": str}`, where `seq` is the sequence of the last record folded in. A record stamped later than `now` is left for later rather than skipped, so an earlier snapshot still picks it up when it is restored at a later time.

`restore(snapshot, now)` starts from `data` and replays only the records whose `seq` is greater, and raises `ValueError` when `now` is earlier than `snapshot["now"]`. The snapshot is believed rather than checked, which is what lets the log be rewritten underneath it.

`compact(snapshot, now)` rewrites the log as one line beginning `state ` whose payload is the codec text of `{"seq": ..., "state": ...}`, followed by the framed records whose `seq` is greater, and returns `load(now)`. It removes the history at or below that sequence, so a snapshot older than the compaction cannot be restored.

examples.code:
j = CheckedJournal()
j.append("a", 1, now=0)
j.append("b", 2, now=1)
print(j.load(5))
snapshot = j.snapshot(1)
j.remove("a", now=2)
print(j.restore(snapshot, 5))
print(j.load(5))
examples.explanation: The snapshot covers both records and names the last sequence it folded in. Restoring starts from that state and replays only the tombstone that came after, matching what a full replay gives.

examples.code:
j = CheckedJournal()
j.append("a", 1, now=0)
j.log[0] = j.log[0].replace('"a"', '"z"')
try:
    print(j.load(5))
except ValueError as error:
    print(type(error).__name__)
examples.explanation: The payload changed but the checksum in front of it did not, so the line is refused. The base journal would have replayed the altered record without noticing.

examples.code:
j = CheckedJournal()
for value in range(6):
    j.append("k" + str(value), value, now=value)
before = j.load(10)
snapshot = j.snapshot(2)
print(len(j.log))
print(j.compact(snapshot, 10) == before)
print(len(j.log))
print(j.load(10) == before)
examples.explanation: Six records become a state line plus the three the snapshot does not cover, and the state is unchanged. The saved snapshot still points at the same data afterwards.

persist:followup.approach: Put the checksum in front of the payload and split the line on the first space, so the reader never has to trust a length it computed from the data it is checking. That buys two refusals instead of one: a payload that does not match its checksum, and a line with no newline at all. Refusing the torn tail is the judgement call worth arguing for. The base journal dropped it because an unterminated line was the only visible sign of an interrupted write; once every line carries a digest, an unterminated line is still just an unterminated line, and silently dropping it is how a log loses the write you most wanted to keep. Cover the version inside the payload so the checksum covers it too, otherwise a downgrade passes the check. The bigger change is the position. The base problem counted lines, which is fine until compaction rewrites the log and the count stops pointing where it did. Number every record as it is appended and let the snapshot carry the sequence of the last record folded in, then a position names a record rather than a place in a file, and compaction can replace the prefix with one state line without invalidating anyone at or after it. Say plainly what compaction still costs: the history below the sequence is gone, so compact towards a snapshot you intend to keep rather than the newest one every time.
persist:followup.note: A checksum covers the bytes, not the intent. It catches a record that was damaged after it was written; it cannot tell you a record is missing, only that what is there is what was written. And a torn tail is now refused rather than dropped, because a line nobody can vouch for is not a record.

sheet.overview: A spreadsheet is only trustworthy if the arithmetic under it is right, so start with the language: one pass to turn text into tokens, a recursive descent parser, and an evaluator that refuses rather than guesses. What a write invalidates is the next stage, and being precise about what this stage cannot do is what makes that stage obvious.
sheet.task: Implement `Sheet` with `get`, `set` and `evaluate`, over cell references, literals, the four operators and the five aggregate functions.
requirements: A cell is letters then digits: `A1`, `B2`, `AA10`. Rows start at 1, so `A0` is rejected, and a name like `nonsense` is not a cell at all.
`set` takes a number or a string starting with `=`. Any other value, including a `bool`, a list or a plain string, raises `ValueError` and changes nothing.

Formulas allow cell references, integer and float literals, `+ - * /`, parentheses, unary minus, and `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `AVG`, `COUNT` over ranges like `A1:B4` or lists like `SUM(A1:B2,D1:D2)`. Precedence is the usual one and unary minus binds tighter than `*` and `/`, so `=-A1+4` is `4 - A1`.
A function argument is a cell or a range. An unknown name, a trailing token such as `=2 3`, an unbalanced bracket and `SUM(A1*2)` all raise `ValueError` rather than being quietly reinterpreted.
A reversed range such as `B2:A1` raises `ValueError`. The ends are never silently swapped, and a range with only one end, such as `=A1:`, is refused too.
Whitespace between tokens is ignored, but nothing else is: a character the grammar does not recognise is an error rather than something to skip.
`get` on a cell that was never set returns `0`, and an unset cell reads as `0` inside a formula too, so `COUNT(A1:B2)` on a fresh sheet is 4 and `SUM(A1:B2)` is 0.
Division by zero yields the string `"error"`. Any formula that reads an error cell yields `"error"` as well, including a function whose range contains one.

Nothing is recomputed. A write is one evaluation against the values as they stand, so a formula that reads its own cell sees the value that cell held before the write, and a cell written afterwards leaves the cells that read it alone. Tracking what depends on what is the next stage.
`evaluate(formula)` runs one formula against current values, stores nothing, and needs the leading `=`.
The parser records every reference it sees while it parses, so the dependency list for a formula is a by-product of the parse rather than a second pass over the text.

examples.code:
s = Sheet()
s.set("A1", 2)
s.set("A2", 3)
s.set("B1", "=(A1 + A2) * 10")
s.set("C1", "=-A1 + 4")
s.set("D1", "=2 + 3 * 4")
print(s.get("B1"))
print(s.get("C1"))
print(s.get("D1"))
examples.explanation: Precedence and nesting come from the grammar, and unary minus binds tighter than multiplication so it applies to A1 alone.

examples.code:
s = Sheet()
s.set("A1", 1)
s.set("A2", 2)
s.set("B1", 3)
s.set("B2", 4)
s.set("AA1", 10)
s.set("AB1", 20)
s.set("C1", "=SUM(A1:B2)")
s.set("C2", "=AVG(A1:B2, AA1:AB1)")
print(s.get("C1"))
print(s.get("C2"))
print(s.evaluate("=COUNT(A1:B2)"))
examples.explanation: A multi-letter column is just base 26 with a 1-based digit, so AA1 is column 27, and AVG over six values divides once.

examples.code:
s = Sheet()
s.set("A1", 3)
s.set("B1", "=A1 * 10")
print(s.get("B1"))
s.set("A1", 7)
print(s.get("B1"))
s.set("B1", "=B1 + 1")
print(s.get("B1"))
examples.explanation: One write is one evaluation against the values as they stand, so B1 keeps its 30 when A1 changes. Knowing what depends on what is the next stage. Rewriting B1 reads the 30 it already held, which is why the last line is 31 and not 1.

examples.code:
s = Sheet()
s.set("A1", 1)
s.set("B1", "=A1 / 0")
print(s.get("B1"))
s.set("C1", "=COUNT(A1:B1)")
print(s.get("C1"))
try:
    s.set("D1", "=SUM(A1:A2")
except ValueError:
    print("refused")
print(s.get("D1"))
examples.explanation: Division by zero is a value, not an exception, and it poisons every formula that reads it, a function over its range included. A malformed formula is a different thing entirely: it is refused, and the cell it named keeps the value it had.

sheet.approach: Tokenize in one pass, deciding at each character whether it starts an operator, a number, a cell reference or a function name, and raise there rather than later: a character you decide to ignore becomes a number you are confident about. If the tokenizer finds matches by pattern rather than by walking the string, compare the matches back against the source, because the pattern skips what it cannot match and a silent skip is the same failure by another route. Then parse by recursive descent, one method per precedence level, so `2 + 3 * 4` cannot come out as 20 and `-A1` binds to A1 alone. Keep every cell as a (row, column) pair rather than as its text: a pair compares, so the ends of a range decide its order and a reversed range is caught with one comparison, and expanding `A1:B4` into cells becomes arithmetic instead of string work. Evaluate as you parse the value in, and judge division before you divide so the error is a value every reader can see. Nothing here caches or recomputes, and that is deliberate rather than lazy: one write is one evaluation, and a stage that pretends to know about dependencies without a graph teaches the candidate to guess at them. Recording the references during the parse is the one piece of foresight worth making now, because it is free at this stage and it is exactly what the next stage needs.
sheet.note: Two traps hide here. First, a reversed range: `B2:A1` has to raise rather than swap its ends, because swapping invents a range nobody asked for and quietly returns a number. Second, argument position: if a function argument accepts an expression, then `SUM(A1*2)` becomes a question about something other than what it looks like, so restrict arguments to cells and ranges. Reading an unset cell as `0` everywhere keeps the two consistent with each other: `SUM` over a blank block is 0 and `COUNT` over that same block is the number of cells in it.

sheet:followup.overview: A total that is quietly stale is worse than one that is briefly wrong, so the next stage is about invalidation: writing one cell must cost what depends on that cell and nothing more. Two maps do it, read in opposite directions, and batching shows where the atomicity argument really has to be made.
sheet:followup.task: Build `BatchSheet`: the base engine plus a dependency graph, so a write recomputes only its transitive dependents, a cycle is refused, and a batch of writes lands whole or not at all.
requirements: `get`, `set`, `evaluate` and the formula syntax behave exactly as in the base problem: the same `=`, the same operators and functions, the same `"error"`, the same `ValueError` for a malformed formula or a reversed range.
`set(cell, value)` is one write and returns the cell's new value. `set_many(changes)` applies a whole dict of writes and returns the number of formula cells it evaluated.
A write recomputes only the transitive dependents of the cell it wrote, and only those. `recomputations` counts formula evaluations, and both `set` and `set_many` move it.
A cell that was never written reads as `0`, exactly as in the base.
A write that would create a cycle, including a cell reading itself, raises `ValueError` and leaves every value and the counter untouched.

`set_many` parses the whole batch and proves it acyclic before anything lands, so a `ValueError` leaves the sheet exactly as it was. Two writes that only close a cycle together, such as `{"A1": "=A2", "A2": "=A1"}`, are still rejected.
A cell that several writes reach is evaluated exactly once, however many times it appears in the dirty set.
`order(changes)` returns the same dirty cells, as addresses such as `"B1"`, in an order where every cell comes after the cells it reads. It writes nothing and does not move `recomputations`.
A constant written in the batch still invalidates its dependents; a formula cell written in the batch is itself dirty and is evaluated in that same pass.
An error cell is still a dirty cell: it stays in the plan and is re-evaluated when its input is repaired.

examples.code:
b = BatchSheet()
b.set("A1", 1)
b.set("A2", 10)
b.set("B1", "=A1 * 2")
b.set("C1", "=B1 + A2")
b.set("D1", "=100")
before = b.recomputations
b.set("A1", 5)
print(b.recomputations - before)
print(b.get("C1"))
print(b.get("D1"))
examples.explanation: Only B1 and C1 depend on A1, so exactly two evaluations happen and D1 keeps its value. That is the whole point of the graph: the cost of a write is what depends on it.

examples.code:
b = BatchSheet()
print(b.set_many({"A1": 1, "B1": "=A1 * 2", "C1": "=B1 + 1"}))
print(b.get("C1"))
examples.explanation: Three writes land together. B1 and C1 both carry new formulas, so both are dirty and both are evaluated, each exactly once.

examples.code:
b = BatchSheet()
b.set_many({"A1": 1, "B1": "=A1 * 2", "C1": "=A1 * 10", "D1": "=B1 + C1"})
before = b.recomputations
print(b.set_many({"A1": 2}))
print(b.get("D1"))
print(b.recomputations - before)
examples.explanation: D1 reads two cells that both changed. Recomputing it once per input would be two evaluations and one wasted answer.

examples.code:
b = BatchSheet()
b.set("A1", 1)
b.set("B1", "=A1 / 0")
try:
    b.set("A1", "=B1 + 1")
except ValueError:
    print("rejected")
print(b.get("A1"))
print(b.get("B1"))
print(b.order({"A1": 5}))
examples.explanation: The refused write would have closed a loop through B1, so the sheet is left exactly as it was, error cell included. order answers the same question without writing: only B1 depends on A1.

sheet:followup.approach: Keep two maps and no more: what each formula reads, and who reads each cell. One is the other turned round, so storing both is a cache rather than a second source of truth, and the same two maps answer two questions in opposite directions. On a write, replace the edges leaving the cell being written and walk its dependents depth-first, appending each cell as the walk finishes it, then reverse that list. Reverse finish order is the topological order, and the reversal is the part that matters: handing the list over unreversed publishes a total before the formula it feeds, which is precisely the stale number nobody forgives. The cycle check reads the same maps the other way round, because a new formula closes a loop exactly when one of the cells it reads already reaches it by reading. Do all of that before touching any state, so the rejection costs nothing. Batching is where atomicity shows up, so split `set_many` into a prepare phase and an apply phase: prepare parses every value and rebuilds the edges on copies of the live maps, then runs the cycle test against those copies, which is what catches a cycle that only exists because two writes were considered together. Once prepare returns, nothing can fail, so apply assigns the new maps wholesale and evaluates the plan. The plan is the same depth-first post-order filtered to formula cells and seeded from every written cell, which gives evaluated-once for free, because a cell is entered once however many paths reached it. Sort the seeds so the plan does not depend on the order the caller happened to write the dict in.
sheet:followup.note: The cycle check has to run against the post-batch graph, not the live one. Checking each write on its own misses `{"A1": "=A2", "A2": "=A1"}`, where neither entry is a cycle until both are applied, and applying them one at a time would leave the sheet holding the first half of a write that was supposed to be atomic. The other invariant worth writing down is that an error is not a tombstone: an error cell is still a dirty cell, so it stays in the plan and is re-evaluated when its input is repaired.

sql.overview: A query layer is where a key-value store either becomes usable or becomes a source of wrong answers. The hard part is not finding rows, it is making the answer a function of the data rather than of the order writes happened to arrive in, which means pinning down what a missing value means and where a tie goes.
requirements: A row is a dict with an integer `key` column. Values are numbers, strings or `None`, which is what keeps every ordering total.
`insert` replaces a live key and resurrects a deleted one, so the key space stays one key space. It raises `ValueError` on a missing or non-integer key and on a value of another type.
`update` merges into a live row and returns it, or returns `None` for a missing or deleted key. A column outside `schema(table)` and any change to `key` raise `ValueError` and write nothing.

`delete` writes a tombstone: the row leaves every query, `include_deleted` still shows it as `(key, None)`, and `history` lists every version in write order with `None` per delete. Deleting an absent or already deleted key is a no-op.
`select` filters with `where(row)`, where an absent column reads as `None`. With no `order_by` rows come back in ascending key order, and every returned row is a fresh copy.

Ordering by a column ranks a missing value first, then numbers before strings, then the value, and breaks ties on ascending key. `desc` reverses the whole finished list, so it is the exact mirror of ascending.
`limit` keeps the first rows of that order and must be `None` or a nonnegative integer; a negative limit raises `ValueError`.
`schema(table)` is the sorted union of every column ever seen in that table, and columns are never renamed or dropped.

examples.code:
s = TableStore()
s.insert("users", {"key": 3, "age": 40})
s.insert("users", {"key": 1, "age": 30})
s.insert("users", {"key": 2, "age": 25})
print(s.select("users", where=lambda r: r["age"] >= 30))
print([r["key"] for r in s.select("users")])
examples.explanation: Insertion order was 3, 1, 2. The default order is by key, not by arrival, and rows come back as copies.

sql.approach: Store one record per key, as a row and a deleted flag, rather than removing the key from the map. A delete then costs a flag write and every read path checks that flag, which is what keeps history reconstructable without a second structure to keep in step. Keep a per-table set of every column ever seen, because that set is what turns a typo in `update` into an exception instead of a new column nobody else agrees exists. For ordering, give every column value a rank rather than comparing values directly: a row with no value gets a rank of its own and so never reaches a value comparison, and numbers rank before strings so a mixed column sorts instead of raising on the first pair. Then append the key to that rank, and one sort key gives you missing-first, type ordering, ties broken by key and a stable result in one expression. Finish by reversing the sorted list for `desc` rather than flipping each comparison, so descending is provably the mirror of ascending and the tie rule needs no second statement. Hand back copies of every row, or a result you already hold will change under you after the next update.
sql.note: The two judgement calls worth defending explicitly. A missing value sorts before every present value in ascending order, which makes `desc` put the present values first and means `limit` takes real data rather than blanks unless you ask for the opposite; the alternative, sorting blanks last, hides them behind an arbitrary sentinel and makes the first page of a limit-ordered query empty on a sparse column. And re-inserting a deleted key resurrects it rather than failing, because a key space that splits into live and deleted halves is a much harder thing to reason about than a delete that a later write can undo. Either choice is defensible; what matters is that you state it and that the tests hold you to it.

sql:followup.overview: Aggregates are the first queries where the answer can depend on the order writes arrived in rather than on the data. A single row read cannot betray that, but a group list can, and a counter that disagrees with the rows it counted is worse than a slow query.
sql:followup.task: Extend the store with `count`, `group_by` and `group_count`, keeping the base insert, update, delete, select and schema rules unchanged.
requirements: Keys are integers and values are numbers, strings or `None`. `insert` requires the `key` column, `update` rejects a column outside `schema(table)` and any change to `key`, and `delete` writes a tombstone no query can see.
`select` still returns fresh copies in ascending key order by default, with the same missing-first ordering rule and the same `desc` and `limit` behaviour.
`count(table, where=None)` counts live rows only. A tombstone is not a row with a missing value, so it is never counted.
`group_by(table, column, where=None)` returns `(group, rows)` pairs sorted by group, with the `None` group first, and each group's rows in ascending key order. Rows are copies.
A row with no value for the column, or one that stores `None` there, belongs to the `None` group. It is never dropped from the aggregate.
`group_count(table, column, where=None)` returns the same groups as `(group, n)` pairs, and the group sizes must add up to the matching `count`.
The group order must not depend on the order rows were written or the order the predicate kept them.

examples.code:
g = GroupedStore()
g.insert("t", {"key": 1, "team": "a"})
g.insert("t", {"key": 2, "team": "b"})
g.insert("t", {"key": 3, "team": "a"})
print(g.group_count("t", "team"))
print([r["key"] for r in g.group_by("t", "team")[0][1]])
examples.explanation: Groups come out sorted by group value rather than in the order the first row of each group arrived, and each group is ordered by key.

sql:followup.approach: Do not build a parallel aggregate structure. Compute the grouping from the live rows on each call and sort the result, which costs one extra sort but removes a whole class of bug where a cached count drifts away from the rows it counted. Reuse the base ordering rank: it already answers "missing first, numbers before strings", so a group with no value sorts ahead of every real group and a group list reads the same way a `select` does. Bucket on the raw value, including `None`, so a row with no column lands somewhere defined rather than vanishing from the total. Derive `group_count` from `group_by` rather than counting separately, then assert that the sizes add up to the count, because two counters over the same rows are exactly the pair that will disagree after the first delete or group-value update. Sort inside each group on the key so the rows are reproducible, and return copies so a later update cannot rewrite a result someone is still holding.
sql:followup.note: Keep the three ways of being absent strictly separate, because they are the whole difficulty. A row with no value for the group column belongs to the `None` group. A row with the column set to `None` also belongs to the `None` group, which is why the rank function treats them identically. A tombstone belongs to no group at all, so it must be filtered before bucketing rather than turned into a `None` group member: bucket first and a deleted row quietly resurrects itself as a phantom group.
